scope_note: 3.2 owns packet simulation: longest prefix match, route-source selection by administrative distance, and metric comparison within a protocol. Items that only read a field belong to 3.1.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. A workstation sends traffic to a file server at 10.20.30.55. Which interface does R1 use to reach that server?

exhibit.content:
R1# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       N1 - OSPF NSSA external type 1, N2 - OSPF NSSA external type 2
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       i - IS-IS, su - IS-IS summary, L1 - IS-IS level-1, L2 - IS-IS level-2
       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP
       a - application route
       + - replicated route, % - next hop override

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 6 subnets, 4 masks
C        10.1.1.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
C        10.1.2.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.1.2.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
O        10.20.0.0/16 [110/65] via 10.1.1.2, 00:10:04, GigabitEthernet0/0
O        10.20.30.0/24 [110/74] via 10.1.2.2, 00:10:04, GigabitEthernet0/1

options.text: GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/1
The packet is dropped.
Both interfaces, load-shared.

items.explanation: A router forwards using the most specific matching entry. 10.20.30.55 is matched by both 10.20.0.0/16 and 10.20.30.0/24, and the /24 is longer, so R1 uses its next hop 10.1.2.2 out GigabitEthernet0/1. Option A follows the /16 entry and ignores longest prefix match entirely, the single commonest forwarding error. Option C assumes no match exists when two entries in fact match. Option D treats the two overlapping entries as equal-cost paths, but load sharing requires the same prefix, not merely overlapping ones.

exhibit.content:

       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area

       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2

       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP
       a - application route
       + - replicated route, % - next hop override

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 6 subnets, 3 masks
C        10.1.1.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
C        10.1.2.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.1.2.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
O        10.40.32.0/20 [110/65] via 10.1.1.2, 00:22:41, GigabitEthernet0/0
O        10.40.48.0/20 [110/65] via 10.1.2.2, 00:22:41, GigabitEthernet0/1

options.text: GigabitEthernet0/0
The packet is dropped; no gateway of last resort is set.
GigabitEthernet0/1
Both interfaces, because the two /20 entries overlap.

items.explanation: A /20 covers sixteen values in the third octet. 10.40.32.0/20 therefore spans 10.40.32.0 to 10.40.47.255, and 10.40.48.0/20 spans 10.40.48.0 to 10.40.63.255. The destination 10.40.48.10 falls in the second block, so R2 forwards out GigabitEthernet0/1. Option A places .48 inside the first block, a boundary error of exactly one /20. Option B ignores that a matching entry exists. Option D assumes the two blocks overlap, but consecutive /20s are disjoint.

Options A and B pick specific entries whose prefixes do not contain the destination at all, an error that comes from scanning for a familiar-looking row rather than testing containment. Option C forgets that 0.0.0.0/0 matches every destination, which is precisely why the header reports a gateway of last resort.

options.text: It discards the packet, because no entry in the table matches the destination.
It floods the packet out every interface except the one it arrived on.
It forwards the packet out GigabitEthernet0/0 as a best-effort attempt.
It forwards the packet toward the numerically closest network in the table.

items.explanation: No entry covers 172.31.9.4 and the header confirms that no gateway of last resort is set, so R4 has nowhere to send the packet and drops it. Option B applies switch behaviour for unknown unicast frames to a routed lookup, which never floods. Option C invents a best-effort default that IOS does not implement. Option D assumes numeric proximity between addresses matters, but a lookup tests prefix containment, and 172.31.9.4 is not contained by any entry shown.

exhibit.content:
R5# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       N1 - OSPF NSSA external type 1, N2 - OSPF NSSA external type 2
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       i - IS-IS, su - IS-IS summary, L1 - IS-IS level-1, L2 - IS-IS level-2
       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP
       a - application route
       + - replicated route, % - next hop override

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 6 subnets, 4 masks
C        10.1.1.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
C        10.1.2.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.1.2.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
D        10.50.0.0/16 [90/2172416] via 10.1.1.2, 00:19:37, GigabitEthernet0/0
O        10.50.7.0/24 [110/65] via 10.1.2.2, 00:19:37, GigabitEthernet0/1

options.text: GigabitEthernet0/0, because the EIGRP entry's distance of 90 beats the OSPF entry's 110.
GigabitEthernet0/0, because the EIGRP entry's metric is the larger of the two values.
GigabitEthernet0/1, because /24 is a longer match than /16 for that destination.
Neither; R5 drops the packet because two protocols advertise overlapping prefixes.

items.explanation: Both entries are already installed for different prefixes, so administrative distance has nothing left to decide. The lookup picks the longest match: 10.50.7.99 falls inside 10.50.7.0/24, so R5 forwards out GigabitEthernet0/1. Option A applies administrative distance across two different prefixes, the central misconception this item targets; distance only breaks ties between sources offering the same prefix. Option B compares metrics from different protocols, which are never comparable. Option D invents a conflict where the two entries coexist normally.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R6 is also receiving a RIP advertisement for 192.168.100.0/24 with a hop count of 2. Which statement explains which route R6 installs in its routing table?

exhibit.content:
R6# show ip route 192.168.100.0
Routing entry for 192.168.100.0/24
  Known via "ospf 1", distance 110, metric 65, type intra area
  Last update from 10.1.1.2 on GigabitEthernet0/0, 00:07:41 ago
  Routing Descriptor Blocks:
  * 10.1.1.2, from 3.3.3.3, 00:07:41 ago, via GigabitEthernet0/0
      Route metric is 65, traffic share count is 1

options.text: The OSPF route, because its administrative distance of 110 is lower than RIP's 120.
The RIP route, because a hop count of 2 is numerically lower than an OSPF cost of 65.
Both routes, because R6 load-shares whenever two protocols offer the same prefix.
The RIP route, because its updates arrive more often than OSPF link-state refreshes.

items.explanation: When two sources offer the same prefix, IOS compares administrative distance first and installs the more trustworthy source. The exhibit prints distance 110 for the OSPF entry, and RIP's 120 is higher, so the OSPF route stays. Option B compares a hop count with an OSPF cost, but metrics from different protocols have no common scale. Option C invents cross-protocol load sharing, which does not occur. Option D substitutes update frequency for distance, which plays no part in route selection.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. A static route for 192.168.60.0/24 is configured, yet the routing table shows only the OSPF entry. Which statement describes R7's forwarding behaviour for that prefix?

exhibit.content:
R7# show running-config | include ^ip route
ip route 192.168.60.0 255.255.255.0 10.9.9.2 130
R7#
R7# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       N1 - OSPF NSSA external type 1, N2 - OSPF NSSA external type 2
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       i - IS-IS, su - IS-IS summary, L1 - IS-IS level-1, L2 - IS-IS level-2
       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP
       a - application route
       + - replicated route, % - next hop override

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        10.9.9.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.9.9.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
O     192.168.60.0/24 [110/74] via 10.9.9.2, 00:41:55, GigabitEthernet0/0

options.text: OSPF forwards the traffic now; the static route installs only if the OSPF route is withdrawn.
The static route forwards the traffic, because static routes always outrank dynamic ones.
Traffic is shared between the OSPF next hop and the statically configured next hop.
The static route is rejected as invalid, because 130 exceeds the maximum usable distance.

items.explanation: The trailing 130 sets the static route's administrative distance above OSPF's 110, making it a floating static. The better-trusted OSPF entry is installed and the static waits in reserve, appearing only if OSPF withdraws the prefix. Option B assumes statics always win, which is true only at their default distance of 1. Option C would require equal distance and equal cost. Option D treats 130 as out of range, but the configurable distance runs to 255, and 130 was chosen deliberately.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Both paths from R1 to 192.168.70.0/24 are inside OSPF area 0. Which path does R1 install, based on the costs shown?

options.text: The path through R2, with a total cost of 21.
The path through R3, with a total cost of 11.
Both paths, because OSPF always load-shares across available paths.
The path through R2, because it has the lower administrative distance.

items.explanation: OSPF sums the outgoing interface costs along each path. Through R2 the total is 10 plus 10 plus 1, which is 21; through R3 it is 5 plus 5 plus 1, which is 11. The lower total wins, so R1 installs the path through R3. Option A adds the costs correctly but then selects the higher total. Option C assumes load sharing without checking that the costs are unequal. Option D invokes administrative distance to separate two routes learned from the same protocol, where it is identical and decides nothing.

options.text: It forwards the packet to 203.0.113.1 out GigabitEthernet0/0 using the default route.
It forwards the packet out GigabitEthernet0/1 toward the 192.168.1.0/24 network.
It queues the packet until a more specific route for 192.168.90.0/24 is learned.
It discards the packet, because the longest match points to Null0.

items.explanation: 192.168.90.0/24 is a static route to the Null0 interface, and it is a longer match for 192.168.90.5 than the 0.0.0.0/0 default, so it wins the lookup. Traffic sent to Null0 is silently discarded. Option A applies the default route despite a more specific entry existing. Option B picks an unrelated connected network that does not contain the destination. Option C invents queueing behaviour; a router that resolves a lookup to Null0 drops the packet immediately rather than holding it.

Option A treats table order as a tie-break, but listing order carries no preference. Option B invents an interface-number tie-break that IOS does not apply to installed paths. options.text: GigabitEthernet0/0, because the OSPF entry has the better administrative distance.
GigabitEthernet0/1, because a /32 host route is the longest possible match.

items.explanation: A /32 host route matches exactly one address, and it is the longest match available for 10.60.5.7, so it beats the covering 10.60.0.0/16 and the packet leaves by GigabitEthernet0/1. Option A compares administrative distance between two different prefixes, where prefix length decides instead. Option C ignores that overlapping matches are resolved by length rather than left as a choice. Option D confuses this static host route with the L entries IOS creates for a router's own interface addresses.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R14's routing table also holds a 10.70.0.0/16 entry learned through OSPF. What does this output confirm about how R14 forwards a packet addressed to 10.70.20.5?

exhibit.content:
R14# show ip route 10.70.20.5
Routing entry for 10.70.20.0/24
  Known via "ospf 1", distance 110, metric 83, type intra area
  Last update from 10.1.1.2 on GigabitEthernet0/0, 00:11:03 ago
  Routing Descriptor Blocks:
  * 10.1.1.2, from 4.4.4.4, 00:11:03 ago, via GigabitEthernet0/0
      Route metric is 83, traffic share count is 1

options.text: R14 will use the 10.70.0.0/16 entry, because it was learned earlier.
R14 will drop the packet, because two entries overlap for that address.
R14 will use the 10.70.20.0/24 entry, the longest match for that address.
R14 will alternate between the /16 and /24 entries on successive packets.

items.explanation: Querying show ip route with a host address makes IOS report the entry that address actually resolves to, and it names 10.70.20.0/24 rather than the covering /16, confirming the longest match. Option A treats age as a tie-break, but the table stores no such preference between different prefixes. Option B assumes overlap is an error, when overlapping entries are normal and resolved by length. Option D invents per-packet alternation, which happens only between installed equal-cost paths for one prefix.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R15 receives advertisements for 172.20.40.0/24 from both EIGRP and OSPF, and the OSPF advertisement carries a cost of 3. Why did R15 install the entry shown rather than the OSPF one?

exhibit.content:
R15# show ip route 172.20.40.0
Routing entry for 172.20.40.0/24
  Known via "eigrp 100", distance 90, metric 3072, type internal
  Last update from 10.8.8.2 on GigabitEthernet0/1, 00:03:12 ago
  Routing Descriptor Blocks:
  * 10.8.8.2, from 10.8.8.2, 00:03:12 ago, via GigabitEthernet0/1
      Route metric is 3072, traffic share count is 1
      Total delay is 20 microseconds, minimum bandwidth is 1000000 Kbit
      Reliability 255/255, minimum MTU 1500 bytes
      Loading 1/255, Hops 1

options.text: Because EIGRP updates arrive faster than OSPF LSAs, so EIGRP populated the table first.
Because the EIGRP route is internal, and internal routes are always preferred over OSPF.
Because metrics are compared only when two routes carry the same prefix length.
Because administrative distance is compared first, and EIGRP's 90 beats OSPF's 110.

items.explanation: The exhibit prints distance 90 for the EIGRP entry. When two protocols offer the same prefix, IOS compares administrative distance before it ever looks at a metric, so EIGRP wins and the OSPF cost of 3 is never weighed against 3072. Option A substitutes timing for distance. Option B invents a rule about internal routes that would apply within EIGRP, not between protocols. Option C states a condition that is already satisfied here, since both advertisements carry the same /24.
